extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners advising on interference/derivation matters)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive guidance for USPTO examiners (and practitioners) on when and how to suggest, require, conduct, and act after interferences and derivation proceedings, including priority showings, claim requirements, secrecy orders, estoppel, and Board interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to add claim to provoke interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner may, pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 132(a) and 37 CFR 41.202(c), require an applicant to add a claim that would interfere with the claim of another application or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim the examiner proposes to have added must (1) be patentable to the applicant, and (2) be drawn to patentable subject matter claimed by another applicant or patentee. The requirement may be made to obtain a clearer definition of the interfering subject matter or to establish whether the applicant will pursue claims to the interfering subject matter. When requirement is based on a published application with allowed claims or a patent, the examiner must identify that published application or patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: When interfering claim already in application
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant already has a claim to the same subject matter as a claim in the application or patent of another inventor, there is no need to require the applicant to add a claim to have a basis for an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner may invite the applicant to suggest an interference under 37 CFR 41.202(a). If the applicant does not, the examiner should work with an Interference Practice Specialist (IPS) to suggest an interference to the Board, including an explanation why at least one claim of every application or patent defines the same invention per 37 CFR 41.203(a), and must complete Form PTO-850.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner preparedness to discuss interference issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should be prepared to discuss why claims interfere, whether other claims would have been anticipated or rendered obvious if the interfering claims are treated as prior art, and whether an applicant or patentee is entitled to claim the benefit of an application as a constructive reduction-to-practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IPS may require the examiner to prepare a memorandum for the Board on any of these subjects and may require the examiner to participate in a conference with the Board to discuss the suggested interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary principles for requiring an interfering claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the cost and complexity of interferences, a requirement to add a claim under 37 CFR 41.202(c) should not be lightly made. Before making the requirement, the examiner should consult with an IPS. The following principles should guide the examiner's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles: (A) Generally do not suggest an interference if examination is not otherwise completed. (B) The required claim must not encompass prior art or otherwise be barred. (C) The application must provide adequate support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for the subject matter of the required claim. (D) A claim should not be required when the applicant expressly states the commonly described subject matter is not the applicant's invention. (E) A claim based on a claim from a published application should not be required unless the claim from the published application has been allowed. Examples provided illustrate application of these principles (e.g., pre-AIA 102(b) prior art, time-bar situations, attribution to another inventor, genus/species relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and content of form paragraph to require adding claim (Form ¶23.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 23.04 may be used to require an applicant to add a claim to provoke interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required claim must be copied exactly in the form. Applicant is given TWO (2) MONTHS from mailing date to add the claim; refusal to add will operate as concession of priority for the subject matter of the required claim but will not abandon the application. Extensions may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136(a) but cannot carry the reply beyond the six-month statutory maximum (35 U.S.C. 133). If interference would be with a patent, applicant must also comply with 37 CFR 41.202(a)(2)–(a)(6). Examiner notes indicate bracketed insertions (e.g., published application number or patent number) and other drafting instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of refusing to add required claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to add a required claim will operate as a concession of priority for the subject matter of the required claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant would be barred from claiming the subject matter of the required claim and any subject matter that would have been anticipated or rendered obvious if the required claim were treated as prior art (see In re Ogiue). While complying, an applicant may still express disagreement in several ways; the examiner may withdraw the requirement if persuaded by applicant's reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections based on disclaimer (failure to present claims for interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected on the ground that the applicant has disclaimed the subject matter involved, which may arise from failure to present claims or take necessary steps for interference purposes after notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of such failures: (A) not making claims suggested for interference under 37 CFR 41.202(c); (B) not copying a claim from a patent when suggested; (C) not responding or appealing within the fixed time to an examiner's rejection of claims copied from a patent. The rejection on disclaimer applies to all claims not patentably distinct from the disclaimed subject matter as well as to the claims directly involved. Rejections based on disclaimer should be made using form paragraphs 7.48.aia, 7.48.fti, and 7.49, with examiner notes on bracket insertions and preconditions for use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership and election of priority
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative patent judge may decline to declare, or the Board may issue judgment in, an interference between applications or patents that are commonly owned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference is rarely appropriate between two applications or an application and patent that belong to the same owner. The owner should determine priority and is obligated under 37 CFR 1.56 to inform the examiner which application or patent is entitled to priority. The examiner may require an election of priority; the owner must eliminate commonly claimed subject matter by canceling claims, disclaiming patent claims, amending application claims, or filing a reissue to amend patent claims. Examples (e.g., post-merger applications, co-inventor disagreements) illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show priority under 37 CFR 41.202(d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever an application has an earliest constructive reduction-to-practice later than the apparent earliest constructive reduction-to-practice for a patent or published application claiming interfering subject matter, the applicant must show why it would prevail on priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no showing has been filed and the applicant's earliest constructive reduction-to-practice is later, the examiner must require a showing of priority because an insufficient showing (including none) can trigger a prompt judgment against the applicant (see 37 CFR 41.202(d)(2)). The showing must, if unrebutted, support a determination of priority in favor of the party making the showing. When testimony or production necessary to show priority is not available without authorization under §41.150(c) or §41.156(a), the showing must include any necessary interrogatories/requests/deposition requests and a detailed proffer of expected responses and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship to 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily an applicant may use an affidavit under 37 CFR 1.131 to overcome a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(e); however, an exception arises when the reference is a patent or a published application that has claims directed to the same patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the reference contains claims directed to the same patentable invention as the application claims being rejected, priority is determined in an interference and the applicant must make the priority showing under 37 CFR 41.202(d) instead of using a 1.131 affidavit. The examiner should consider whether an interference would be possible at the time the affidavit would be submitted; if not (e.g., published claims significantly modified or not in condition for allowance), a 1.131 affidavit may be permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority showing is not a priority statement; sufficiency and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A priority showing presented during examination under 37 CFR 41.202(d)(1) is not the same as a priority statement filed during an interference; it must actually prove priority assuming the opposing party does not oppose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inadequate showing can have serious consequences: if an interference is declared and the Board finds the priority showing insufficient, the applicant will not be allowed to present additional evidence to make out priority unless the applicant shows good cause for not presenting it earlier. Case law cited includes Kistler v. Weber, Huston v. Ladner, Hahn v. Wong, Edwards v. Strazzabosco, Basmadjian v. Landry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy order cases (interferences and secrecy orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference will not be declared involving a national application under a secrecy order; although an applicant under secrecy may suggest an interference, the Office will not act while the application remains under secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An interference should not be suggested for an application under a secrecy order because an opposing party is entitled to access the application once an interference is declared. When a secrecy order expires or is rescinded and examination is otherwise complete, the need for an interference may be reconsidered. If a non-secret application has allowable claims that interfere with allowable claims of a secret application, the non-secret application should be passed to issue; an interference may be suggested once the secrecy order is lifted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board jurisdiction and examiner action during an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board acquires jurisdiction over any involved file when it initiates a contested case; other proceedings for the involved file within the Office are suspended except as the Board may order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a patent or application becomes involved in an interference, the Board has jurisdiction over the file and the examiner may not act on an involved patent or application except as the Board authorizes. The Board may consult the examiner on technology questions and retains jurisdiction until the interference is terminated (termination defined by Director after final Board judgment and exhaustion of judicial review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on ex parte communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte communications about an inter partes reexamination or about a contested case with a Board member or a Board employee assigned to the proceeding are not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because interference involves two or more parties, integrity requires the opportunity for communications or actions regarding any involved application or patent. Any attempt by a party to communicate with the Board through the examiner or to have the examiner act in an involved patent or application without Board authorization should be promptly reported to the Board. Board action may include sanctions or referral to the Office of Enrollment and Discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to related files during contested proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Any request from a party for access to or copies of Office records directly related to a contested case must be filed with the Board and must precisely identify the records (copies require appropriate fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access and copies will ordinarily only be authorized for: (1) the application file for an involved patent; (2) an involved application; and (3) an application for which a party has been accorded benefit under subpart E. Opposing party access under 37 CFR 41.109 is separate from public access under 37 CFR 1.11/1.14 and has no bearing on those public-availability provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of related examinations and minimizing adverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the examiner may not act in a patent or application directly involved in an interference, examination may continue in related cases, including benefit files; suspension of related cases may be necessary in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once examination is completed, the examiner should consult with an IPS to determine whether and how further action should proceed. Suspension may be necessary if claims would be barred by a loss in the interference. Steps to minimize the effect (e.g., on patent term adjustment) should be considered: require restriction under 35 U.S.C. 121 to claims that do not interfere so they can issue, while the applicant files a divisional for interfering claims which may be suspended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding additional parties to an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: During the course of an interference, if the examiner discovers other applications or patents of parties that claim the same invention but are not already involved, the examiner should consult with an IPS and prepare a referral of the suggested interference to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the referral in the same way as an initial referral; consult IPS for scope and explanation why the additional files claim same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board action on related files
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may order that a paper be filed in a related application to notify the examiner of a fact relevant to examination of the related case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a paper will generally notify the examiner of a fact (e.g., a party admission or prior art) that may be relevant; examiner should act on Board-ordered filings as directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner responsibilities after an interference (judgment effect within the Office)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Board judgment disposes of all issues that were, or by motion could have properly been, raised and decided. Jurisdiction over an application returns to the examiner once the interference has terminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a recommendation for further action in the judgment, the examiner must reopen prosecution to consider the recommendation, enter any recommended rejection, and maintain the rejection unless overcome by amendment or new evidence. In the first action after termination, the examiner should make of record all references not already of record which were pertinent to preliminary motions and discussed in the decision on motion. An interference judgment resolves priority between parties but does not prevent the examiner from making rejections in further examination. Adverse judgment against a claim is final Office action; if no claim remains allowable, issue a notice of abandonment. Form paragraph 23.02 may be used to resume ex parte prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding or amending claims during an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may file a motion during the interference to add or amend a claim; a patentee may file a reissue application in support of such a motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A copy of the paper adding or amending the claim will be placed in the official record of the application but not entered. The examiner may enter the added claim or amended claim into the application only if, and only to the extent, authorized by the Board (typically in the decision on the motion). The decision authorizing entry does not prevent the examiner from rejecting the claim during further prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel within the Office (merits and procedural estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party loses on an issue in the interference, it may not re-litigate the issue before the examiner or in a subsequent Board proceeding; two main types of interference estoppel exist: merits estoppel and procedural estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merits estoppel: a losing party is barred on the merits from seeking a claim that would have been anticipated or rendered obvious by subject matter of the lost count. Procedural estoppel: a losing party is barred from seeking relief in the Office that could have been--but was not--sought in the interference. The examiner should consult with an IPS before allowing a claim to a losing party that was added or amended during post-interference examination. Numerous examples illustrate applications (e.g., continuing applications claiming subject matter lost in the interference must be rejected as estopped; generic claims encompassing lost subject matter are estopped on merits; procedural estoppel applies even if the applicant later attempts to show the claim did not correspond to the count unless prevented by the Board from making the showing).
